result.delta_one_sentence: A is a broad mechanistic study of how gated linear-attention and delta-rule models store, keep and read bindings, using an exact state decomposition, donor-recipient patching, load varied separately from distance, and key-overlap interference tests, with hybrids as a contrast; B asks one narrow causal question: how much of the recall lost when a passage is split into more tokens comes from the extra decay those tokens add, tested by clamping per-token log-decay back to its canonical sum.
result.reasoning:
Shared ground: both study pretrained recurrent models with a fixed-size state and data-dependent decay. Both run associative recall built into encyclopedia text, score it by likelihood over four candidates, and try to pull elapsed context apart from other causes of forgetting. That is where the overlap ends. The thing each one manipulates is different, and so is the claim it supports.

A takes the general memory system apart. Its exact decomposition of the state into contributions from earlier positions separates three things: retention, storage and access. Patching between paired inputs then finds where a fact is written into the state and where it is read out. A changes the number of active bindings at a fixed length, and the distance at a fixed number of bindings, as two separate factors. Aligning or orthogonalizing later keys against the target's write direction tests directly whether interference depends on key overlap. In hybrids, A shows that recall moves to the attention cache. Each of these tools can be reused, and the findings apply beyond a single setup.

B holds content and bytes fixed and changes only the number of recurrent updates, by re-tokenizing the passage. A per-layer, per-head clamp then makes each canonical token's summed log-decay match its canonical value. B is rigorous: it has a preset 3-point line per unit of log token ratio, a ladder that adds more canonical text up to the same token counts, a boundary perturbation that keeps the token count, a silenced-write arm, a decay ledger, and uniform halving of decay rates.

But B's question is narrow: how much of a tokenization-length penalty comes from decay. The clamp also has an identification weakness. Rescaling the decay changes how the delta rule's extra erasures interact with the state, and re-tokenized text is out of distribution. That makes the leftover share, labeled "everything else", hard to interpret, and a result below the line tells us little. B is the cleaner causal test of one sub-question. A makes the larger and more general contribution, though it risks spreading too wide and producing some expected results, such as hybrids relying on attention. On balance A is stronger.

largest_defect: Identification and decisiveness of the registered kill reading (both reviewers; the identification and feasibility refuters). The primary statistic beta pools K = 1 and K = 4 with equal weight, and at K = 1 the three foils are fresh codes absent from the episode, so recall is a presence test that is likely at ceiling in every arm; gate I4 has floors only, no ceiling. With the registered estimator, a true K = 4 decay secant exactly at the 3-point line reads KILL with probability 0.955 / 0.776 / 0.636 at discordance 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.3 (reviewer 1's rerun; feasibility refuter 0.95 / 0.80 / 0.66), against the registration's stated false-kill rate of 0.05-0.11. Separately, the clamp's natural indirect effect is a patching NIE (= PIE + INT, 2606.27510) evaluated at the re-segmented writes, so it absorbs the decay-by-write interaction: in S1's own worlds the pure decay cost at canonical writes is 17-45 points against registered NIE of 8-14 (INT about -8 to -32), and the 'decay share' is defined by the clamp itself. Both push toward KILL, the owner's expected reading (prior 0.60), and KILL leads to the same action as not running the step (close D20 citing 2609.33093). Further unsimulated pieces of the same defect: the f_p fallback (S1 and S2 hard-code f_p = 2.7; W3 seed 43 would fall back to 2.0, where P(KILL | beta = 0) drops to 0.66-0.81), discordance beyond S2's 0.30 (S1's clamp discordance 0.36-0.45), the 3-point exact-match line carried to forced-choice units without calibration, and passage-level clustering over at most 120 WikiText-103 articles. Repair (one versioned v2): drop K = 1 from the primary pool or use in-episode foils, add a ceiling gate and re-size n; add a DECAY-ONLY arm at canonical writes and report PIE, NIE and INT, reading KILL only if both upper bounds sit below a line recalibrated in forced-choice units (otherwise rescope to the oracle decay-parity effect at re-segmented writes); re-run S1 (multi-layer, state-dependent writes) and S2 through primary_f over every reachable f_p and discordance up to 0.5 with article-level clustering.

largest_defect_by_reviewer.reviewer_1: The registered decisive reading is biased toward the expected KILL and cannot give the upper bound it was designed for. beta weights K = 1 and K = 4 equally. At K = 1 the three foils are fresh codes that never appear in the episode, so the test only asks whether the code was seen, and that is probably at ceiling in every arm. S1's toy has no channel for "was the code present" and cannot show this. There is also no ceiling gate, and the line of 3 is carried over without calibration from the dossier's exact-match r = 2 slope. As a result, a true K = 4 decay secant exactly at the line reads KILL with probability 0.955 / 0.776 / 0.636 at discordance 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.3. I got these numbers by rerunning the registered estimator.cluster_normal and decide_subject at n = 1,500 per load. The registration states a false-kill rate of 0.05 to 0.11. Fix: drop K = 1 from the primary pool, or use foils that occur in the episode; add a ceiling gate; recalibrate the line in forced-choice units; re-run S1 and S2 through primary_f. My review also raised a second issue, about transfer. Normalizing per ln f mixes up how much extra decay the gates give out-of-distribution fragments (R_F) with how much that decay costs. KILL should be conditioned on median R_F >= 1.5, and a decay-dose arm should be added at canonical tokenization. (1) The proposal concedes the point. It says it "claims no new mechanism and no new method family" (proposal L27-30) and calls itself "a recombination and a measurement, not a new mechanism" (L316-317). The merged discovery verdict is NARROWED, the dossier scores its novelty residual 4/10, and the expected result is KILL, which both closest priors already predict (L168-170).

(2) The protocol comes from Lee et al. 2609.33093. It uses the same m-a-p GDN-1.3B checkpoint at the same commit 930ed6ae (App. A; lee.txt L1023-1025), WikiText-103 passages, K facts, four-candidate likelihood scoring with source passages as clusters (Sec. 2.3), the elapsed-context (filler) arm and the load sweep. Lee's finding that "memory load has a substantially larger effect than elapsed context alone" (Sec. 4.2; lee.txt L759-763) is the hypothesis this step expects to confirm.

(3) "Decay versus interference" comes from Boesch and Wee 2609.16183, with GDN and RWKV-7 cells. They report decay has no measurable cost (0.561 vs 0.518, p = 0.86; boesch.txt L633-636) and attribute the distance wall to interference.

(5) The per-token decay clamp is the only claimed delta (L271-273: patching the decay channel with the canonical decay summed over each token's pieces). It is Tallec and Ollivier's time-warping invariance condition (1804.11188, Eqs. 6-7, read in full: the gate g(t) = dc/dt, so per-step forgetting must shrink by the local stretch factor), imposed by hand on the decay term only. S4 (2111.00396, read in full, L810-812) did the uniform version at inference: "simply by changing its internal step size Delta" for 0.5x-frequency input. This project's own legacy D20 already had the per-span version, "span oracle: g'_t = g_t / r_s" (legacy/directions/20-semantic-clock-gate-parity.md L34), and the forgetting-mass ledger F(s_L)/F(s_en) that becomes R_F. The proposal's novelty ledger does not credit the span oracle as the clamp's origin.

(6) Reading clamp-minus-native as a natural indirect effect is textbook activation-patching mediation: Vig et al. 2004.12265, Imai et al. 2013, and Lee's own state and write patching on the same checkpoint. 2606.27510 (found by my q1, not cited in the proposal) re-derives exactly this NIE estimand from activation patching.

result.closest_prior_mechanism_paragraph: Pretrained linear-attention language models with a fixed-size recurrent state (data-dependent multiplicative gating, with or without a delta-rule update, at a small and a medium size), plus hybrids that add full-attention layers, read controlled associative-recall inputs: one or more key-value bindings embedded in natural-text passages from a public encyclopedia corpus, followed by a query; recall is scored among four balanced candidate values by conditional likelihood, with the target logit margin as a continuous measure and source passages as the statistical unit. The state at any position is decomposed exactly into the contributions of earlier positions, each transformed by all later transitions, which separates retention from storage and access. Causal interventions patch states, writes and query-time read components between paired donor and recipient inputs that differ only in the bound value, to locate where a fact enters the state and where it is read. Memory load (the number of active bindings at fixed sequence length) is varied separately from elapsed context (natural filler tokens between the fact and the query at fixed load), and later writes have their keys aligned with or orthogonalized against the target's write direction to test whether interference depends on overlap; retention, targeted editability and collateral damage are tracked as load grows. In hybrids the same interventions show that recall is carried by the attention cache rather than the recurrent state.

result.mechanism_paragraph: Two pretrained language models without attention, whose only memory is a fixed-size recurrent state updated by a gated delta rule (one with a scalar decay per head and a short convolution, one with a decay vector per channel and an in-context removal term), read English episodes: K facts binding a noun phrase to a random 4-digit code, a 512-token passage of encyclopedia text, and a query; recall is scored by forced choice among four candidate codes from their string likelihoods. The passage is re-tokenized into 1.5, 2.0 or 2.7 times as many tokens by splitting each canonical token into smaller in-vocabulary pieces, so its bytes and content are unchanged while the number of recurrent updates grows; facts, query and codes keep their canonical tokens. In a paired arm, the per-position decay of the re-tokenized passage is rescaled at every layer and head (or channel) so that the summed log-decay over each canonical token's pieces equals the log-decay that token received in the canonical run of the same episode, leaving the extra writes and erasures, the convolution or token shift and the unfamiliar segmentation as they are. Recall in this clamped run minus recall in the native re-tokenized run is read as the part of the re-tokenization cost carried by the extra decay mass, per unit of log token ratio, against a preset line of 3 points at loads of 1 and 4 facts; the remainder is attributed to everything else. result.delta_one_sentence: A holds bytes fixed and asks one causal question: when finer tokenization adds recurrent updates and hurts recall, is the cause the extra decay or the extra writes? It answers with a 2x2 decay-mass transplant that decomposes the cost exactly. B builds a general mechanistic map of recurrent-state memory, using exact per-position state decomposition, write/state/read patching, load separated from elapsed context, key-overlap interference, editability and hybrids, to locate where facts are stored, kept and read.
result.reasoning:
Both designs use the same setting: gated linear-recurrent (delta-rule) models with a fixed-size state, facts embedded in encyclopedia passages, and four-way likelihood recall. Both care about separating retention (decay) from write interference. They are still different mechanisms, because the core lever of each is missing from the other. A's lever is re-tokenization at fixed bytes plus transplanting decay mass between canonical tokens and their pieces, which gives an exact additive decomposition of total cost into decay, write and interaction terms. B's lever is exact unrolling of the state into per-position contributions plus activation patching, with separate manipulations of load, elapsed context and key-direction overlap.

A is crisper and more falsifiable. It has a preregistered threshold, a kill rule and an exact accounting identity. But its scope is narrow: how tokenizer granularity interacts with decay. It also has a validity gap. Non-canonical splits into in-vocabulary pieces are off-distribution for the pretrained model, so the 'write' term mixes extra-update cost with tokenization-shift cost. Rescaled decays are also states the model never produced in training. The secondary arms (canonical lengthening, uniform decay scaling) only partly address this.

B is broader and more reusable. It separates storage, retention and access; it tests a specific interference hypothesis by orthogonalizing write keys; it covers several architectures including a larger model; and its result about attention-cache dominance in hybrids generalizes beyond one tokenization question. B's risk is diffuseness and a heavier analysis load, but as a contribution it explains more and gives the field tools. A would be a strong focused note. B would be the more significant paper if executed well.

Identification.strongest_argument:
KILL is the verdict that closes D20, and it is produced by the R_F guard and the line's normalisation, not by what decay does. The registered rule returns KILL with probability 1.00 in three worlds whose mechanism truths are opposite:
- (a) decay is causally inert (S1v2 W7, DOSE 0.0);
- (b) the fact-carrying unit's gate fully self-normalises (R_F 1.00) while a per-token clock would cost 42.4 corrected points per log-f;
- (c) gates partially self-normalise everywhere (R_F 1.55) while a per-token clock would cost 13.7 per log-f, 4.6 times the line.

The only arm that tells these worlds apart is DOSE, and DOSE is descriptive (L8): it cannot change the reading.

The cause is in the wave-1 repair for "KILL where decay cannot act" (proposal repair table, row 4). That repair added a guard, `decide_subject` with RF_MIN = 1.5, which takes a scalar "median R_F over split tokens pooled over layers and heads or channels" (registration v2, Readouts). The pool has three problems:
1. It is unweighted. It counts every layer-head unit (GDN, 24 x 8) or layer-channel unit (RWKV-7, 24 x 2048), whether or not that unit holds a fact across a 512- to 1,382-token passage.
2. In Mamba-family models, most units are local. LongMamba (arXiv 2504.16053, ICLR 2025, read in full) says "most channels, termed local channels, focus on local contexts". It also says the global channels are "primarily responsible for Mamba's long-context capability".
3. The registration already defines retaining channels for I5 (canonical passage-total decay factor at least 1e-3) but does not apply that definition to R_F.

So the guard measures the local units, which hold none of the facts. If the memory units self-normalise and the local units do not, TNIE and PNIE are about 0 because there is no excess decay where the facts are, and the rule reads KILL. The correct reading is SELF_NORMALIZED. KILL's consequence then states something false ("with the gates charging fragments at least 1.5 times canonical decay") and closes D20. SELF_NORMALIZED would instead send any successor to a natural-text R_F ledger. The program decision flips on how many irrelevant units are pooled.

Separately, b_TNIE and b_PNIE are divided by 0.75 ln f_p, the token fertility, not by the decay dose actually delivered. At an R_F just above 1.5, both contrasts are about a sixth to a seventeenth of the per-token-clock cost, so a decay pathway that costs several times the line still reads KILL.

Neither simulation can see either problem:
- S1v2 has two units. Both carry facts and both share one lambda, so the pooled median always equals the memory units' R_F. Its only partial world, W6, has a large decay scale and reads MATERIAL.
- S2v2 takes R_F as an exogenous scalar input (1.1 or not) and never computes it from units.

Novelty.strongest_argument:
I refute on the trivial-recombination prong. I found no direct prior. My 9 counted queries turned up nothing that runs this measurement, and neither did the 147 counted queries before them. So the verdict is NARROWED, not OCCUPIED. But the repair did not make the recombination less trivial. It added more published parts, and the one step the proposal still calls new already has published analogues that it does not cite.

(1) The proposal concedes the frame. It "claims no new mechanism or method family: it is a measurement" (L417-420). It calls the factorial 2606.27510's noising and denoising pair "with the alignment across unequal segmentations as the only new step" (L349-351). Its ledger says "no new estimator" (L399).

(2) The decomposition is textbook and uncredited. TE = PNIE + PNDE + INT is VanderWeele's three-way decomposition (Epidemiology 2013, doi 10.1097/ede.0b013e318281a64e): direct, pure indirect and mediated interactive effects. The 4-way version is VanderWeele 2014 (doi 10.1097/ede.0000000000000121). The repair tried to search for this twice (r08, r14), both calls failed with HTTP 429, and the claim registry C01-C46 has no VanderWeele entry. Setting the mediator to its value under the other treatment is the crossover design of Imai et al. 2013, which is cited but read only as an abstract. So the 2 x 2 design copies the field's standard estimand.

(3) The "only new step", aligning decay mass across sequences with different token counts, has published inference-time versions in pretrained recurrent models:
- LongMamba (2504.16053, ICLR 2025, Sec. 5.2, Eq. 13; full text read) is a training-free method on pretrained Mamba LMs. It aligns each global channel's cumulative decay (the product of A-bar) over a longer input with the cumulative decay the channel learned at the training length. This is the clamp's operation, with sequence-level rather than per-token granularity, used as a fix rather than as a mediator patch.
- Zhan et al., Exploring Token Pruning in Vision SSMs (2409.18962, NeurIPS 2024, Sec. 4.1, Eqs. 5-6, Algorithm 1; full text read), is "pruning-aware hidden state alignment". Pruned positions keep their decay (state = state * dA) but drop their writes, so fewer writes carry the longer sequence's decay mass. That is structurally the DEC arm. They also show that removing those decay positions costs accuracy in pretrained models.
- Task-Synchronized RNNs (2204.05192) resample a trained GRU's gates in time with no retraining. Hirschi (2604.02474) time-warps a pretrained LSTM's time scale by editing a few parameters. Both apply the Tallec-Ollivier condition at inference, on top of S4's uniform version (2111.00396) that the proposal already credits.
None of these four is cited. LongMamba was named by the wave-1 novelty refuter and is still missing from the registry and from the "decay rescale" family (L365-372).

(4) The remaining credited parts are unchanged:
- the protocol, checkpoint, passages, four-candidate likelihood, load and filler arms come from Lee et al. 2609.33093;
- the question in words, decay against interference, comes from Boesch and Wee 2609.16183;
- same-content re-segmentation comes from 2506.19004, 2607.26831 and 2603.10771;
- the R_F ledger and the span oracle come from legacy D20;
- activation-patching mediation comes from 2004.12265 and 2404.03646.
The idea of a decay-by-input interaction (INT) also has theory behind it: 2111.03282 argues that reading a forget gate as a time scale fails when inputs keep arriving. The cited Oberauer and Lewandowsky make the cognitive-science version.

(5) The expected outcome is one the priors already predict. In the owner's forecast (registration v2 L525-529), MATERIAL has 0.05; KILL, MASKED, SELF_NORMALIZED and PARITY_NULL together have 0.60. The proposal says KILL is "the same closure" as not running the step (L196), that it extends Lee et al. "not overturn[s]" them (L317-322), and of Boesch and Wee that "the question is theirs" (L341-343). So the residual is one new cell in an existing table: a known perturbation, crossed with a known decay-mass alignment, read through the standard three-way decomposition, inside a copied protocol, with a forecast that the priors already cover.

Best case against me: nobody has run PNIE, TNIE and INT on real attention-free checkpoints under same-content re-segmentation. Lee never intervenes on decay. Boesch and Wee ablate decay only during training. S1v2 shows that INT can be large and of either sign, so a clamp-only study would mislead. That makes the measurement new and better identified. It does not make it more than a direct combination of published parts.
